data.title: Is AI Mode killing the internet’s search-based business model?
data.description:
When AI chatbots burst onto the scene, there was chatter that they would kill Google search and the surrounding business models. 

The latest fiscal results are shedding some light on this prediction, and it seems that it is indeed affecting publishers and companies depending on Google search traffic. 

Google, in a bid to stay ahead of chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude, launched its own AI mode. 

However, that is creating another problem, as more users use AI mode instead of visiting the websites providing the information. 

There was a simple business model. Google crawled and indexed websites and displayed those links to users and directed traffic towards publishers. 

Those visits provided advertising revenue, attracted subscribers for higher-value information and allowed websites to build audiences. 

Artificial intelligence is challenging this model. 

Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode provide users with information directly on search-result pages, reducing the need to click through to individual websites. 

The consequences are beginning to appear in company earnings.

Reddit reported a sharp decline in search referrals.

Freelance platform Fiverr also highlighted the impact of AI-related disruption on traditional search engine optimisation (SEO) work. 

Google is also facing challenges in generating advertising revenue from AI mode compared to revenue from conventional search.

The development raises a broader question about the sustainability of the open internet. 

If websites lose the traffic that finances their content, what happens to the information that AI models themselves depend on?

Industry executives believe the shift could represent a lasting change in the economics of the internet, with implications for publishers, companies and users. 

Google’s AI transformation is changing the economics of search

Google started AI Mode as an answer to ChatGPT.

ChatGPT’s introduction made companies question whether conversational AI would eventually replace a search engine.

The initiatives appear to be generating greater engagement. 

Google reported its highest query growth in five years. 

However, increased search activity does not necessarily translate into higher traffic for websites or greater advertising revenue for Google.

Alphabet’s third-quarter results highlighted this. 

The company reported search growth of 12%, down from 19% at the beginning of the year, while search and advertising revenue fell short of Wall Street expectations.

Google also warned of further pressure on search-revenue growth in the fourth quarter.

Another indication of the changing economics is the deceleration in paid-click growth. 

Google’s paid clicks increased 13% year over year in the first quarter, but the growth rate slowed to 8% in the third quarter.

AI Mode could be contributing to this shift.

Unlike conventional search, where users typically encounter several links and advertisements before visiting a website, AI Mode attempts to provide a more comprehensive response within Google's own interface.

This creates a different user experience. Consumers can ask follow-up questions, compare information, and explore topics without necessarily leaving Google.

For the search giant, the challenge is converting that engagement into revenue. 

For publishers, the problem is users tend to stay with Google’s AI Mode and end up not visiting their sites. 

Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, acknowledged during the company's earnings call that AI Mode currently generates lower monetisation than traditional search, despite recording more queries.

Google is attempting to address the issue by expanding advertisements in AI Mode to additional countries and experimenting with new advertising placements as conversations progress.

Reddit's traffic decline offers an early warning

The consequences of this changing relationship are becoming particularly visible among websites that have historically depended on Google for audience acquisition.

Reddit is one of the clearest examples.

The platform's shares plunged approximately 29% on October 30 after its third-quarter results and outlook disappointed investors.

Investors were particularly concerned about weaker-than-expected user growth and the deterioration in search referrals.

Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search traffic had declined by more than one million referrals per week during October.

He also warned that daily active users coming from search could decline by more than 10% in the fourth quarter.

Huffman suggested that Google's AI Overviews were becoming a more prominent part of the search experience, pushing traditional website links further down the results page.

“What started as a feature is now the full search experience,” he said during the earnings call. “And, at a minimum, it pushes everyone down the search page. And then, on top of that, the experiences themselves are not traffic drivers.”

He added that users continued to want Reddit's content, but Google was no longer directing visitors to the platform at the same rate.

"Google is crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either. The reality is, the AI mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody," Huffman said on the post-earnings call.

The distinction is important because Reddit's business model benefits from user engagement, conversations, and the extensive archive of discussions available on its platform.

Historically, Google helped introduce new users to those discussions. 

AI-generated answers can now provide information extracted from similar conversations without requiring users to visit Reddit.

The platform is responding by tightening access to its content. 

Reddit said it would begin trialling a requirement for users to log in to access the website in international markets before the end of the year.

The move is intended partly to restrict AI bots from scraping its content.

Publishers face a weakening incentive to produce free content

The problem extends beyond Reddit.

Fiverr CEO Micha Kaufman described the changes as an earthquake across the internet, arguing that organic clicks were declining as more consumers turned to AI assistants to find information.

“The internet as we’ve known it for the past 20-plus years is going away, and it’s going to completely change,” Kaufman said. “It’s dying.”

Fiverr's third-quarter revenue declined 15.8% from the year-earlier period.

In its shareholder letter, the company highlighted the impact of AI-related disruption on traditional SEO services, saying the changes had affected both low-value and high-end work on its platform.

The development could have broader consequences for digital publishing.

Many online businesses depend on organic search traffic to attract readers and generate advertising impressions. 

Others use search referrals to acquire customers, promote subscriptions or direct visitors towards commercial products.

When AI-generated summaries answer questions directly, fewer users may reach the original websites.

Monica Tartau, Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs, believes this represents a structural rather than temporary change.

“It looks more permanent than temporary to me,” Tartau told Invezz.

She argued that the traditional relationship between Google and publishers is changing because the search engine increasingly answers questions itself rather than directing users to the websites providing the underlying information.

Expert view

Google used to send people to websites. Now it answers the question itself (AI Mode & AI Overview) and keeps them there. It still needs the web for material, but it doesn’t need to send users to it the same way.

Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs
Monica Tartau

According to Tartau, this weakens the financial incentive for websites to continue producing freely accessible information.

“A lot of sites made money or justified the work because people clicked through from Google,” she said.

The expert added that when AI mode provides the answer before the user clicks, “that page view, ad, signup, or sale often doesn’t happen.”

The problem is particularly relevant for businesses that rely on large volumes of relatively inexpensive content and organic search traffic.

AI search could undermine the information it depends on

The potential consequences extend beyond the immediate financial pressure on publishers.

AI search engines rely on information produced across the internet. 

News organisations, specialist publications, research platforms and independent websites contribute material that helps AI systems answer questions.

If those publishers lose the revenue that finances their work, the supply of original information could deteriorate.

Michael Heinrich, CEO of 0G, described this as one of the more serious long-term risks associated with AI-powered search.

“Producing original information costs money,” Heinrich told Invezz.

Expert view

Whether you're running a newsroom, conducting scientific research or publishing specialist industry analysis, someone has to fund the work. If AI systems consume that information while reducing the audience publishers can monetize, eventually the economics stop making sense for some of them

CEO of 0G
Michael Heinrich

. 

Heinrich expects publishers to respond in different ways. 

“Larger publishers can negotiate licensing agreements, specialist platforms may move behind paywalls, and smaller independent sites could simply publish less,” the expert noted.

That creates a potential feedback loop.

“The problem for AI companies is that they still need a steady supply of accurate, current information. If fewer people are producing original material, AI systems risk drawing from an increasingly repetitive pool of secondary content, including material generated by other AI systems.”

This creates a contradiction for the AI industry. 

The technology could become increasingly effective at extracting and presenting information while simultaneously weakening the financial incentives that encourage people to produce that information in the first place.

Can Google make AI Mode as profitable as traditional search?

If Google backs AI Mode, it needs to find a way to transfer the advertising economics from search to AI Mode. 

In traditional search, a user searching for a particular product or a service can see sponsored links alongside organic results. 

Advertisers can compete for those placements, while Google earns revenue from commercial interactions.

AI Mode offers a different opportunity.

Because users can provide more context and ask follow-up questions, the platform may gain a better understanding of their needs and purchasing intentions.

Heinrich believes this could eventually create new advertising opportunities.

“If a user asks an AI assistant to compare laptops for a particular budget, for example, there's a very clear commercial intent that advertisers would be willing to pay to reach,” he said.

Google has already begun expanding advertisements within AI Mode, including to additional countries and through experiments involving advertisements that appear as conversations continue.

However, integrating advertising into AI-generated answers introduces another challenge: maintaining user trust.

In conventional search, sponsored links are generally distinguishable from organic results. 

Within a conversational AI response, the distinction between an objective recommendation and a paid placement could become less obvious.

Heinrich expects advertising decisions to continue reflecting user intent, relevance, conversion potential and advertiser bids.

But he cautioned that commercial incentives should not determine what an AI system presents as factual information.

If consumers begin questioning whether recommendations are genuinely useful or simply favour advertisers, Google could undermine the credibility of the product it is trying to monetise.

Tartau also noted that Google is already expanding advertisements in AI Mode, but said the company has acknowledged that these placements currently generate less revenue than conventional search advertisements.

She said Google's expectation is that users conducting early-stage research may become more commercially valuable as they continue asking follow-up questions.

For now, however, the ability to generate more interactions has not necessarily translated into equivalent monetisation.

Are paywalls and login requirements a good solution?

As search traffic becomes less reliable, websites are likely to reconsider how they distribute their content.

One option is restricting access through subscriptions, registration requirements, or other forms of login barriers.

Reddit is already planning this. By limiting access, the platform will make it more difficult for AI systems to scrape its discussions. 

Tartau said that for Reddit, “a login stops some of that, gives them a direct relationship with users, and more control.”

However, login requirements are not necessarily an effective solution for every publisher.

Tartau said such restrictions could also prevent casual visitors from discovering a website through search.

For Reddit, the strategy may make sense because its value lies partly in its extensive archive of conversations and user-generated discussions.

For a conventional publisher, the calculation is different.

“But if your business depends heavily on people discovering you through Google, putting everything behind a login can be quite damaging. You're effectively asking people to commit to your platform before they've had an opportunity to understand its value”, Heinrich added.

Experts expect many websites to adopt a middle-ground approach.

Michael Heinrich said there would be a hybrid approach where “publishers keep enough content publicly accessible to attract new readers while protecting premium research, proprietary data or specialist analysis.”

He believes publishers with differentiated content and established audiences could have greater opportunities to negotiate licensing agreements with AI companies.

However, smaller websites that depend heavily on search discovery could face greater difficulties.

The expert also highlighted an important distinction: restricting access through a login wall does not automatically establish ownership rights or prevent every form of AI use.

He added that a publisher's negotiating position will depend on the uniqueness of its information, licensing arrangements and the technical controls used to enforce access.

“Most sites will probably do something in the middle: leave some stuff open so they can still be found, put the better material or tools behind a login, and try to build more direct relationships through newsletters and apps so they’re less dependent on Google,” Monica Tartau added. 

The internet's next business model remains uncertain

Despite the hybrid model’s possibility, there is still uncertainty for the publishers. 

Funding the content that populates the internet is always a challenge. Free information was supported by advertisements driven through clicks. 

As AI models eat up advertisements and clicks, it threatens to close off the internet and make users pay for basic access. 

Key takeaway

The open web only works if someone is still willing to fund the content that lives on it.

Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs
Monica Tartau

The internet's search-based business model is therefore facing more than a decline in clicks. 

It is confronting a fundamental question about who gets paid when information is created, indexed, extracted, and delivered through artificial intelligence.

data.title: Apple stock gains as Bernstein highlights safe-haven appeal amid AI selloff
data.description:
Apple shares rose 0.99% on Friday, even as broader technology stocks came under pressure following Nvidia's decline.

The iPhone maker is increasingly attracting investors seeking exposure to a relatively defensive technology business amid uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, according to Bernstein analysts.

In a report published Thursday, Bernstein analysts led by Mark Newman said Apple had become less correlated with its large-cap technology peers and was increasingly trading alongside high-quality consumer companies.

"With little correlation to tech peers, Apple now trades in line with high quality consumer stocks," the analysts said.

The assessment comes as Nvidia faces leadership uncertainty following reports surrounding CEO Jensen Huang, while concerns about the substantial capital expenditure requirements of AI infrastructure continue to weigh on technology stocks.

Apple gains safe-haven appeal as AI spending weighs on tech

Unlike several other Magnificent Seven companies, Apple has relatively modest capital expenditure requirements.

Its capital expenditure accounts for less than 2% of revenue, compared with the hundreds of billions of dollars being committed by major technology companies to AI infrastructure.

Bernstein described Apple as a consumer compounder, noting that its revenue growth, earnings generation and free cash flow profile increasingly resemble those of established consumer businesses.

The brokerage reiterated its outperform rating on Apple and maintained a $380 price target, implying approximately 7% upside from Thursday's closing price.

Apple trades at around 37 times its expected earnings per share for 2027, roughly twice the broader market's forward earnings multiple.

Among companies with market capitalizations above $200 billion and expected EPS growth below 15%, only Costco, Walmart and General Electric also trade at forward price-to-earnings multiples above 30.

However, Apple's projected annual revenue growth through 2029 is approximately 9%, compared with 7% for Costco and 5% for Walmart.

Bernstein also highlighted Apple's estimated 3.1% free cash flow yield and expected share repurchases equivalent to 3% of its market capitalization in 2027 and 3.2% in 2028.

iPhone demand and services offer growth opportunities

Apple's operating performance continues to provide support for its valuation.

In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, iPhone revenue increased 17% year over year to $57.6 billion, despite supply constraints.

The company reported September-quarter revenue records for iPhone and record upgrades worldwide, including in the US, China and India.

The launch of iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, has expanded its product portfolio and created additional upgrade opportunities.

AI also represents a potential growth driver.

Apple's planned improvements to Siri, including personalized assistance and contextual awareness, could encourage customers to upgrade to newer devices.

The company may also generate additional revenue by offering expanded access to advanced server-based AI capabilities.

Its Services business provides another monetization opportunity.

With more than 2.5 billion active devices worldwide, Apple has a substantial installed base for services such as Apple Pay, iCloud+, Apple Music and Apple TV.

The expansion of bundled services and the introduction of Apple Pay in India and advertising on Apple Maps could support further growth.

Rising memory costs and supply constraints pose risks

Despite its defensive characteristics, Apple faces several operational challenges.

The company expects gross margin to decline to 45%-46% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with 47.9% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.

Rising memory prices and expenses related to Siri AI are expected to contribute to the decline.

Apple also continues to face supply constraints involving advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity and memory components.

While advanced-node constraints are easing, memory shortages could affect Mac and iPad availability during the December quarter.

Regulatory scrutiny of its App Store business model and third-party licensing arrangements presents another risk.

Apple expects Services revenue growth to moderate to 8%-9% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with 10% in the preceding quarter, partly reflecting licensing-related and foreign-exchange headwinds.

These pressures could test Apple's ability to sustain its premium valuation even as investors increasingly view the company as a defensive alternative within the technology sector.

data.title: What is ChatGPT Wallet, how does it work and who can use it?
data.description:
OpenAI has given its AI agents a way to pay. ChatGPT Wallet, unveiled on Friday, lets the company’s “dots” agents complete purchases for users, provided the user signs off on each one.

OpenAI set out the details in a blog post and a help-centre guide.

Built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, the feature starts small, but it is OpenAI’s second attempt in just over a year to take ChatGPT from product research to the checkout.

What is ChatGPT Wallet?

ChatGPT Wallet is a payment feature inside dots, the always-on personal agents OpenAI unveiled at its DevDay conference on 29 September.

Until now, a dot that found a sweater or a hotel room still needed a human to finish checkout. With Wallet, users save a card once, and the agent pays through the merchant’s normal checkout.

Cards saved in Wallet are kept separate from the one that pays for the ChatGPT subscription, and from any prepaid ChatGPT balance.

How does ChatGPT Wallet work?

OpenAI’s guidance describes five stages. The user adds a card through a secure form rather than in the chat, and the bank may ask for verification. The user then asks their dot to find something, such as a hotel for a weekend trip.

Before paying, the dot shows the merchant, items, total, chosen card and any recurring-payment terms. The user approves with a biometric check such as Face ID or Touch ID, creating a record of what was authorised.

Finally, the card network issues a payment token, a substitute card number, security code and expiry date, which the agent enters at checkout. The real card details are never shared with the agent or the merchant, OpenAI says.

OpenAI is not taking a fee on transactions at launch, according to CNBC. The sale is between shopper and merchant, which keeps control of pricing, delivery and returns.

Who can use ChatGPT Wallet?

Wallet is open only to ChatGPT Pro subscribers, whose plans cost $100 to $500 a month. Users must be 18 or over, live in the US and hold an eligible US-issued card with a US billing address. It works only in conversations with a dot.

OpenAI’s help centre lists eligible Chase cards for primary cardholders, alongside Amex, Mastercard and Visa. Virtual cards are not supported at launch.

There is no timetable for Free, Go or Plus users, or for the UK and Europe. Amex’s Luke Gebb told CNBC the narrow rollout was deliberate.

What does it mean for consumers?

The main gain is convenience: an agent can take a purchase from search to payment without the user retyping card details.

OpenAI says shoppers keep their card rewards and protections for eligible disputes, such as a faulty item. Refunds go through the merchant, and unrecognised charges through the card issuer.

There are drawbacks. OpenAI concedes some sites may block agents or flag their purchases as fraud. Amazon stops agents buying on its platform, CNBC reported, and United Airlines said this week it would block third-party AI agents from booking. OpenAI also tells users that a “ready to check out” message does not confirm an order.

Privacy is another consideration. Merchants may still need a name, phone number, email and delivery address, which can be passed on through the conversation.

Longer term, OpenAI wants users to pre-approve purchases within spending limits, categories or time windows, so the agent need not ask each time. It has given no date for that.

Why is OpenAI doing this?

OpenAI says 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week, many of them to research what to buy, and it had nearly 100 million paying users at the end of the third quarter, CNBC reported.

Its first checkout push stalled. Instant Checkout, launched in September 2025 with the Agentic Commerce Protocol built alongside Stripe, was wound down in March, when OpenAI said it lacked flexibility for merchants.

Wallet takes a different route, using merchants’ existing checkouts and the card networks’ token systems. OpenAI is also working with payment firms including Stripe and Adyen, and fraud-prevention specialists such as Forter and Signifyd, so genuine agent purchases are not wrongly declined.

How have markets reacted?

OpenAI is privately held, so attention turned to its listed partners.

At 16:55 GMT, Visa was up 1.4% at $426.20 and Mastercard 1.4% at $661.46 against Thursday’s close, while Amex was 0.5% higher at $319.77, according to Yahoo Finance data.

The moves are modest and cannot be pinned on the launch alone.

What happens next?

OpenAI has published a Commerce Partner Playbook showing merchants how to let its agents through and share product feeds. It says it will widen access once it has learned from early use with businesses, banks and card networks.

data.title: Kraken owner Payward’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA falls 67% as trading volumes slide
data.description:
Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, reported a sharp fall in third-quarter profit from a year earlier, even as results recovered from a weak second quarter.

In its Q3 2026 financial highlights, published on Friday, November 13, the company said adjusted EBITDA was $60 million, up from $23 million in the second quarter. Bloomberg, which reviewed Payward’s shareholder letter, reported that the figure was down 67% year on year.

Payward also changed how it reports. It now uses Total Platform Margin (TPM) in place of adjusted revenue, deducting both the cost of crypto delivered to clients and the staking rewards it pays out. On that basis TPM was $487 million, up 12% from $436 million in Q2 and down 12% from a year earlier.

Volumes down on the year, up on the quarter

Total platform transaction volume was $353 billion, which Payward said was 22% higher than in Q2 but 30% lower than in Q3 2025.

The company said it grew while industry spot volume fell 7% quarter on quarter, citing CoinMarketCap data, and that its share of industry spot volume rose to 6.5% in September from 3.3% a year earlier.

Bloomberg linked the annual decline to softer crypto prices. Bitcoin rallied roughly 40% from mid-August to early October before retreating on inflation worries and concern over how the US midterm elections could affect the industry. Exchanges that depend on trading fees tend to see activity slow when prices fall.

Average assets on platform were $43 billion, down 21% year on year. Payward said that at constant prices they rose 29% to $71 billion, and that clients had added assets in each of the last 12 months.

Less reliance on trading fees

The company is trying to show that its business is no longer just about spot trading. It split TPM into three buckets for the first time:

  • transaction-based TPM rose 7% quarter on quarter to $234 million;
  • asset-based TPM, earned on assets clients hold, rose 26% to $128 million;
  • access-based TPM, from subscriptions, trader evaluations, listings and index licences, rose 7% to $125 million.

Asset- and access-based income together made up 52% of the total, up from 46% a year earlier. Derivatives contracts traded rose 84% year on year to 66 million, billable accounts rose 74% to 1.5 million, and funded accounts rose 37% to 7.1 million. Payward notes that funded accounts are not a count of unique clients, as one client can hold several.

Tokenised stocks, banking and AI agents

Payward said its xStocks tokenised equities business passed $1 billion in assets under management in October and now offers more than 700 tokenised stocks. Earlier this week it added hundreds of UK and EU-listed shares, including the DAX 40.

In the US it plans to offer onchain perpetual futures, starting on Hyperliquid, and single-stock perpetual futures, both subject to regulatory approval. Prediction markets for US clients are listed as a next step, though the company gave no timing. In October it agreed to buy Saldo Bank, an EU-licensed digital bank, with completion subject to regulatory approval.

Payward also named AI as a fifth business pillar alongside trading, banking, asset management and Payward Services. It said every Payward app will get an “agent harness” through which clients can direct AI agents across their holdings, with the first expected early next year. It also plans to launch a personal finance agent, designed to act only within client-set limits and with client approval before a trade runs.

On regulation, Payward said Kraken plans to launch in the UAE following full market approval from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), and that it has received in-principle approval from Kazakhstan’s AFSA.

Bloomberg has previously reported that Payward’s initial public offering may not happen until next year.

For more on the exchange’s fees, products and licences, see our Kraken review. Readers comparing platforms can also check our guide to the best crypto exchanges.

data.title: It's not just Nvidia, IonQ stock is also slipping on leadership shake-up
data.description:
Nvidia isn’t the only technology company facing investor scrutiny over a leadership change.

IonQ (IONQ) stock tanked on November 13 after the quantum computing company announced an immediate executive departure and a reshuffle of its finance team.

The disclosure brings uncertainty just over a week after IONQ raised its revenue outlook – leaving investors weighing fast commercial expansion against management shake-up and the considerable cost of building the business.

Why finance team reshuffle is hurting IonQ stock

In its press release, IonQ said CFO Inder Singh is stepping down immediately, and Gary Merril – the current chief of finance at Commvault – will replace him in early December.

The company also appointed former Juniper Networks’ senior executive Thomas Austin to a newly created chief accounting officer position.

The bearish implication is uncertainty over financial leadership during an expansion that requires careful spending and acquisition integration.

An abrupt transition can make investors demand stronger evidence that execution remains on track.

However, the appointments alone provide no basis for concluding that IonQ Inc faces accounting problems.

Experienced replacements may ultimately strengthen oversight as the business grows.

In short, the sell-off in IONQ stock today reflects uncertainty; where that uncertainty becomes a lasting concern depends on what the incoming team delivers.

Is it worth buying the dip in IONQ shares today?

IonQ shares retain a credible growth case.

The company reported Q3 sales of nearly $174 million, up a whopping 336% year-on-year, and raised its 2026 guidance to $505 million at least.

That said, investors must examine the composition: acquired foundry SkyWater contributed $83.5 million, nearly half the quarterly sales total.

IonQ’s platform segment separately grew a whopping 127% to $90.3 million.

That distinction matters when valuing the stock.

Buying a larger revenue base does not establish how quickly existing operations can expand – or how profitable the combined company will become.

The latest quarter also included a $133.6 million adjusted EBITDA loss.

So IonQ Inc may interest investors comfortable with substantial execution risk, but a lower share price alone doesn’t establish a bargain.

What investors should watch before calling a bottom

IonQ has financial resources to support its ambitions.

It reported $1.7 billion in cash, equivalents and investments at September 30, rising to $3.7 billion on a pro forma basis after October’s $2 billion equity offering.

That financing provides flexibility, although issuing shares dilutes existing ownership.

For prospective buyers, the more useful signals are continued platform growth, progress toward lower operating losses and disciplined integration of acquired businesses.

Clear communication from the incoming finance team would also help investors assess spending priorities.

What’s also worth mentioning is that today’s decline in IONQ shares coincides with weakness in quantum computing stocks at large, so the leadership announcement doesn’t explain every percentage point lost.

IonQ’s challenge is to demonstrate that its expanding business can create durable shareholder value alongside impressive revenue growth.

data.title: Cricket's billion-dollar goldmine: why IPL works and can it rival NFL, NBA, MLB?
data.description:
Most Americans would know, or correctly guess, that football, or soccer, as they call it, is the most-followed sport in the world.

But ask which sport comes second, and there is a good chance their guesses will be wildly off the mark.

In fact, outside the Indian subcontinent and some other Commonwealth countries, many people would struggle to guess the correct answer.

It is cricket, a bat-and-ball game that attracts enormous audiences across densely populated South Asian countries and several other parts of the world.

The India-Pakistan match at the 2019 Cricket World Cup in England attracted an estimated 1 billion viewers worldwide.

That popularity has gradually been transformed into a commercial powerhouse through the Indian Premier League, or IPL, one of the world's biggest sporting leagues that many people outside cricket-playing nations may never have heard of.

How big is the IPL?

There is little that comes close to the Super Bowl in the United States when it comes to sporting events and television audiences.

Nielsen data shows that 125.6 million viewers tuned in to watch the 2026 Super Bowl, in which the Seattle Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots to lift the trophy after 12 years.

Now consider this: an average IPL league match this year attracted 277 million viewers. The final had an even bigger audience of 400 million, according to the official broadcaster.

On a per-match basis, few other sporting leagues come close to the viewership numbers generated by the IPL.

And those eyeballs translate into serious money.

A recent Sportico report valued the Mumbai Indians, the joint most successful IPL franchise, at $2.1 billion.

That puts the team in a valuation league comparable to Major League Baseball's Detroit Tigers and the NHL's Vancouver Canucks, both considered mid-tier franchises in their respective competitions.

Sportico's analysis put the average IPL franchise valuation at $1.7 billion, with almost every one of the 10 teams worth at least as much as some of the lowest-valued franchises in the NHL and MLB.

And the IPL has not even completed two decades of existence.

The four major American leagues have all decorated histories stretching way back into the 20th century.

How did the IPL become so big?

The IPL began in 2008 with the aim of tapping cricket's largely untapped commercial potential.

Eight franchises, some partly owned by hugely popular Bollywood stars, participated in the inaugural edition.

Today, 10 city-based franchises compete in the tournament, with reports of further expansion continuing to circulate.

Every team plays 14 league games, with four top teams advancing to the playoffs.

A total of 74 games are played in a season, far lower than major leagues in America and even Europe.

A strict salary cap is put in place to ensure all teams are on a level playing field.

The cricket-mad Indian public embraced the format, and the league has since grown into a giant in the global sporting business.

The financial transformation has been remarkable. The original eight teams averaged $90 million in value. Sportico's latest calculations put the average franchise valuation at $1.7 billion.

That value is not just theoretical. Recent franchise sales have attracted interest from major global sports investors, including Manchester United owners, American billionaire families, and private equity giants.

Royal Challengers Bengaluru was acquired by a consortium including Blackstone and Bolt Ventures for $1.78 billion ahead of this season.

Another franchise, Rajasthan Royals, was acquired for $1.61 billion by a group that includes Lakshmi Mittal and his family, which also owns a stake in the Boston Celtics.

So what makes these franchises so attractive to investors?

"IPL teams benefit from extreme scarcity with only 10 teams, cost certainty ensuring every team is profitable and potential opportunity in a massive market with a young demographic," Kurt Badenhausen, co-author of the Sportico report, told Invezz.

The combination of a limited number of franchises, a massive potential audience and predictable league economics gives investors exposure to a market that is difficult to replicate.

The money behind the cricket

The financial foundation of the IPL is its lucrative broadcast and sponsorship model.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) sold the league's media rights for ₹48,390 crore, approximately $6.2 billion at the time of the auction, for the 2023-2027 cycle.

That agreement made the IPL the world's second-most valuable sports league on a per-match basis, trailing only the NFL.

But how does that money reach individual franchises?

Venkat Ananth, a longtime sports journalist who runs State of Play, a publication focused on the business of Indian sport, explained that the IPL operates through a central revenue-sharing arrangement.

The BCCI sells media rights to broadcasters and sponsorship rights to commercial partners, then distributes approximately 45%-50% of the proceeds to the teams.

This central pool is critical to franchise economics. Ananth estimates that media-related income accounts for roughly 70% of a team's revenue, while the remaining 30% comes from non-media sources such as ticketing, merchandise and local sponsorships.

For investors, Ananth identifies two major attractions: "One, it is a validation of the Indian consumption story. Two, because of the league's dynamics," he tells Invezz.

The IPL is a closed league, with no promotion or relegation, and has a limited number of franchises. That scarcity, combined with the enormous media rights opportunity and the profile of its owners, makes the teams particularly attractive assets, he said.

The league's growth numbers reinforce that appeal.

The IPL has recorded a compounded annual growth rate of 17.73%, exceeding the growth of all four major American sports leagues as well as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite over the same period.

Sportico's analysis also puts the average IPL franchise revenue multiple at 22.9, the highest among major sporting leagues.

A revenue multiple measures how much a business is valued at relative to the revenue it generates.

In this case, a 22.9-times multiple means the average IPL franchise valuation is equivalent to 22.9 times its annual revenue. Put another way, investors are valuing each $1 of franchise revenue at approximately $22.90.

It is a measure of how much investors are willing to pay for a business relative to its current sales, rather than its profits.

A high multiple can reflect expectations of future growth, but it also means valuations depend heavily on the ability of franchises to sustain and expand their commercial earnings.

A lucrative broadcast deal forms the backbone of what IPL founder Lalit Modi has described as a "recession proof" model.

However, there are questions about whether the next broadcast rights agreement can sustain the league's extraordinary growth.

Can the IPL boom be sustained?

During the last rights cycle, Viacom18, backed by India's second-richest man Mukesh Ambani, and Disney India competed extensively to secure the broadcasting rights, pushing up the value of the deal.

However, the two entities merged in 2024 to form a new broadcaster, JioStar.

The merger created a major player in India's sports broadcasting market, raising questions about whether the next rights auction, due in 2027, will attract the same level of competition and generate an equally lucrative deal.

Ananth believes the next cycle could be challenging, but he also sees an opportunity for franchises to diversify their businesses.

"Yes next rights cycle could be a tricky one but it could also be a blessing in disguise," he said.

Historically, franchises have relied heavily on the central media revenue pool, leaving less incentive to develop other commercial opportunities. Ananth believes that could now change.

"There is a lack of incentive to push the boundaries in terms of going beyond media rights. That is changing, gradually, and with a flat media rights cycle and sponsorship categories such as Real Money Gaming also being vapourised overnight, the hope is that most teams will start taking this bucket seriously."

One example worth watching is the recent partnership between the Mumbai Indians and Nike.

The two signed a multi-year agreement, making Nike the franchise's official kit partner. It marks Nike's first official kit deal with an IPL franchise since supplying the now defunct Deccan Chargers in 2008.

For Ananth, such partnerships reflect how teams are beginning to look beyond broadcasting revenue and develop themselves as consumer-facing businesses.

He believes more franchises are starting to think of themselves as consumer product companies, a shift he considers important for the league's next stage of growth.

The opportunity, he said, is to build something more enduring than media and sponsorship income alone. Teams could develop merchandise, brand partnerships and other commercial products that allow them to recover some of the value potentially lost through a flatter media rights cycle.

But that requires franchises to rethink the experience they offer supporters.

"Teams need to think of it as an experience. Every franchise must own the experience," Ananth said.

That includes everything from the team's visual identity and merchandise design to making products affordable for fans. It also means ensuring that attending an IPL match feels worth the money, with stadium facilities and the overall match-day experience becoming central to the business.

In other words, franchises must become more than teams that play cricket for two months every year. They need to build brands that supporters want to engage with throughout the year.

Can the IPL compete with America's biggest sports leagues?

So can the IPL continue pushing its limits and eventually compete with the biggest American sporting leagues?

Ananth believes the potential exists.

"The conditions are very much there. The television product is good. The gameplay is good," he said.

To become as big as these NFL or MLB or NBA franchises, they (IPL teams) need to do more.

Indian sports journalist
Venkat Ananth

Badenhausen also sees considerable room for growth, although he believes the IPL still has a substantial financial gap to close.

"Its revenue is a fraction of top four American sports leagues, but its valuations are already on par or ahead of the lowest ranked MLB, NHL teams. The IPL has a massive opportunity ahead that could see it continue to close the gap with top American leagues in the decades ahead."

That distinction between revenue and valuation is important.

While the IPL's franchises are already attracting prices comparable to established American sports teams, their underlying businesses still generate considerably less revenue than the biggest US leagues.

The opportunity, therefore, is not simply to sell more broadcasting rights or attract wealthier owners.

It is to turn cricket's enormous audience into a far bigger and sustainable commercial business.

data.title: Why the AI trade is hard to kill, but easy to frighten
data.description:
The artificial intelligence investment boom has developed a familiar pattern: a new threat emerges, technology stocks sell off, and investors soon begin buying the dip.

DeepSeek’s arrival in January 2025 challenged assumptions about the cost of developing advanced AI.

Nvidia fell nearly 17% in a day, losing about $593 billion in market value, before recovering around 8% the next session.

During the tariff turmoil in April 2025, the Nasdaq-100 suffered its fourth-worst two-day loss since 2007, before recording its second-best single-day gain over the same period on April 9, after the White House announced a 90-day pause in reciprocal tariffs.

More recently, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on November 5 as investors worried that Democratic victories in the US midterm elections could slow data-centre construction.

The index rebounded 2.7% on November 9, although falling oil prices also helped lift broader markets.

The rebounds have not erased all losses.

But the sequence captures the trade’s central tension: investors believe AI could transform businesses while questioning the valuations and financing behind it.

Why does the AI trade keep coming back?

For Louisa Loran, an executive adviser and global business strategist who previously worked at Google, the answer begins with demand.

“The AI investment boom has faced several existential threats, but none of them has touched what investors are actually betting on, which is use,” she said.

DeepSeek’s low-cost models raised concerns that cheaper systems could undermine the economics of US AI developers and reduce demand for high-end chips.

Loran argues that lower costs could instead encourage wider adoption.

“DeepSeek made AI cheaper, and lower access cost has always increased uptake in an industry, so it strengthened the case for adoption rather than weakening it,” she said.

Adoption, however, is not yet translating consistently into corporate profits.

A McKinsey survey published in August 2026 found that 80% of respondents said AI had improved individual productivity, while 37% reported at least some contribution to their organisation’s earnings before interest and taxes.

Loran said she had seen this lag while working with Google customers.

“Infrastructure scales at the speed of capital, while returns arrive at the speed at which organisations change how they work and make decisions,” she told Invezz.

Companies may build infrastructure before redesigning processes and training staff to capture its benefits.

Harry Hamann, founder of investment research firm InvestWealth, offered a financial explanation.

He said the market scares had not broken the revenue and cash-flow engines funding the largest technology companies.

The biggest spenders, he argued, have financed much of the build-out from existing businesses, allowing infrastructure orders to continue despite falling share prices.

Hamann separates short-term market movements from longer-term fundamentals.

“Over days, it is mostly positioning: crowded holdings, leverage and options hedging turn a headline into a 5% to 15% move. Over quarters, fundamentals decide, which is why every dip so far has been bought,” he told Invezz.

While Hamann’s framing relies on broad market mechanics rather than a quantitative decomposition of each pullback, it highlights a key divide between short-term trading and long-term capital allocation.

Why are trillion-dollar companies swinging so violently?

The dollar sums involved can make moves appear unprecedented.

A 5% decline in a company valued at $5 trillion erases $250 billion in market value.

But market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by all outstanding shares; a fall in that figure does not mean an equivalent amount of cash has left the stock.

The percentage moves still matter. Franklin Templeton Institute estimated that hyperscalers and AI-adjacent companies together made up nearly 46% of the S&P 500’s market value as of September 30, 2026.

The figure includes companies supplying or adopting AI, not just businesses that sell AI products.

That concentration means a change in sentiment towards AI can affect a significant share of the broader market.

It can also magnify crowded trades, momentum strategies and leveraged positions.

The Bank of England’s July 2026 Financial Stability Report said high concentration, correlated momentum-driven positions and increased leverage could amplify a fall in AI-related share prices if investors reassessed the sector’s earnings prospects.

Options-market data provide a clearer picture of how investor positioning changed as technology stocks came under pressure.

In a November 2 analysis, Cboe Global Markets found that the proportion of stocks among the S&P's top 100 showing inverted call skew — a sign of unusually bullish options sentiment — had fallen from 44% in early October to 10%.

At the same time, retail put buying in mega-cap technology stocks on Cboe's exchanges reached a year-to-date high, accounting for 34% of retail opening trades, compared with an average of 24%.

The figures suggested that investors were moving away from bullish bets on further gains and increasingly seeking protection against potential declines.

That shift became more pronounced during the November 5 sell-off.

In a follow-up analysis published on November 9, Cboe found that increases in S&P 500 put skew and put convexity accounted for 5.5 points of the 11.5-point increase in the VIX that day.

Yet the rise in hedging demand did not translate into widespread expectations of a broader market sell-off.

Cboe's COR1M implied correlation index reached just 22% on November 5, compared with a historical average of around 70% on days when the S&P 500 fell 4% in a session over the previous two decades.

Five of the 11 S&P 500 sectors also finished the week higher.

Cboe said the options market was still pricing a rotation out of AI and technology stocks rather than a broader market contagion.

The data point to a sharp change in investor positioning and demand for downside protection, but do not establish that options trading caused the underlying share-price declines.

These mechanics help explain why a headline can produce a larger move than the immediate change in earnings outlook.

Still, explaining the market mechanics behind violent swings does not prove that underlying valuations are safe from fundamental shocks.

On November 12, Nvidia shares tumbled as much as 14.3% intraday following CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation amid an internal conduct and security probe.

Yet the stock recovered to close down just 4.3% after CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO—while rival chipmakers AMD and Broadcom surged roughly 6% on the day.

That intraday reversal underscored how quickly governance uncertainty can be repriced in a central AI stock without breaking broader appetite for the sector's hardware."

Nor are large percentage declines in major indices unprecedented. The Nasdaq Composite fell 12.3% on March 16, 2020, during the Covid-19 market shock.

What makes today’s moves striking is the enormous market value attached to a concentrated group of AI-linked companies, not proof that markets have entered an entirely new category of volatility.

When does volatility become dangerous?

A share-price fall is not automatically a financial-stability event.

The risk grows if an AI repricing undermines debt used to finance data centres and chips, or spreads losses to lenders.

Professor Iwa Salami, professor of financial law and regulation at the University of East London, said both business concerns and investor behaviour contribute to volatility.

Worries about profits can trigger selling, while crowded ownership, borrowing and rapid efforts to reduce risk can intensify declines and affect the wider market.

Salami said a more serious warning would be companies spending heavily on AI for years without generating sufficient returns.

"Falling profits, mounting debt or a lasting drop in AI investment would be more worrying than a short-term fall in share prices. Regulators should also watch whether losses spread to banks and other financial institutions," the professor told Invezz.

That concern is reflected in official assessments.

A survey of 20 market contacts included in the Federal Reserve's May 2026 Financial Stability Report identified concerns about AI-related equity valuations and capital expenditure increasingly funded by debt.

The report clarified that these responses reflected the views of survey participants, not those of the Federal Reserve Board or the New York Fed.

The Bank of England said AI-related companies' use of credit markets had accelerated rapidly, spanning public markets, private credit, leveraged finance and structured finance.

It described the pace of investment as historically unprecedented, although it found little evidence so far that AI financing was crowding out other borrowers.

It warned that declining hyperscaler free cash flow and increasingly complex financing arrangements could create risks if earnings disappoint or refinancing conditions worsen.

The Bank for International Settlements said financial-stability risks from the AI boom appeared moderate, but warned that its sustainability hinged on companies meeting high earnings expectations.

It also noted that equity prices had moved considerably ahead of debt-market valuations.

The AI trade has so far survived shocks to assumptions about model costs, trade policy and political support for infrastructure.

But resilience should not be confused with immunity.

AI may become more widely used even if some companies have overbuilt, borrowed too heavily or paid too much for infrastructure.

The technology can succeed while particular investments fail.

For investors, the question is whether companies financing AI’s expansion can earn returns that justify the capital committed.

For regulators, it is whether the debt links built around it could transmit a correction into the wider economy.

The next scare may pass, as previous ones have. The test will be whether the cash flows and financing behind the build-out remain intact.

data.title: Microsoft stock steadies after global outage as AI competition intensifies
data.description:
Microsoft shares recovered on Friday after a global outage disrupted its Outlook, Teams and Copilot services, affecting users across more than 70 countries.

The incident has renewed concerns about businesses' dependence on centralised cloud services, while intensifying competition in artificial intelligence adds to the pressure on the technology giant.

Microsoft apologises as outage disrupts services

Microsoft shares MSFT rose approximately 0.18% to $523.94 on Friday, recovering from a decline of more than 2% in premarket trading.

The outage, which began on Thursday, November 12, affected several Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook email, Teams and the Copilot AI assistant.

According to Downdetector, users across more than 70 countries reported disruptions.

The incident affected services used by more than 430 million people, alongside governments and organisations worldwide.

Microsoft engineers worked for more than 20 hours to address the disruption.

In its latest updates, Microsoft apologised for the outage, saying it was "deeply sorry" for the disruption caused since Thursday.

In a 3:05 p.m. EST update, the company said it did not yet have a timeline for full recovery.

Earlier, Microsoft had said it was seeing "broad recovery and stability" across its services.

"Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," the company said in an earlier update.

Microsoft also dismissed speculation that the outage was linked to technical issues involving artificial intelligence agents.

It said the incident was caused by a technical issue and was not related to cybersecurity or AI agents.

The company plans to publish a full post-incident report after completing its review.

Outage highlights dependence on cloud services

The disruption has drawn attention to the risks associated with businesses relying heavily on a small number of major technology providers.

Microsoft's cloud-based model allows organisations to avoid the costs of operating and maintaining their own email servers and infrastructure.

However, a prolonged outage at a major provider can affect large numbers of businesses simultaneously.

Microsoft's second-quarter availability for its Microsoft 365 workplace applications was reported at 99.994% globally, making prolonged disruptions relatively rare.

Nevertheless, the incident could encourage companies to invest more in backup services and continuity arrangements.

Providers such as US cybersecurity firm Mimecast offer continuity services that allow users to send and receive emails through temporary inboxes when their primary systems become unavailable.

Privacy-focused technology company Proton also offers standby email accounts that businesses can activate during disruptions.

According to a study by Oxford Economics and Splunk, unplanned outages of critical digital business systems cost Global 2000 companies an average of $15,000 per minute.

While continuity services have traditionally attracted deadline-sensitive industries such as law, the latest disruption could encourage wider adoption among accounting firms, hospitals and other regulated businesses.

Geopolitical tensions have also increased concerns about dependence on US technology providers, particularly in Europe.

The outage highlighted how technical failures alone can disrupt access to essential digital services.

AI competition adds to pressure on Microsoft

The outage comes at a challenging time for Microsoft as investors assess its position in the artificial intelligence market.

Recent reports about OpenAI's latest figures have raised questions about its competitive position relative to Anthropic.

Microsoft owns a 24% stake in OpenAI and has a smaller investment in Anthropic.

Anthropic also recently introduced a new suite of office tools, adding to competition in a market where Microsoft has a significant presence through its productivity software and Copilot assistant.

Investors will be watching Microsoft's upcoming Ignite conference for updates on its AI strategy and cloud platform Azure.

Citi analyst Tyler Radke said the event could reinforce confidence in the company's AI growth outlook.

"We expect the event to reinforce confidence in Microsoft's AI growth narrative," Radke said in a research note.

The conference could provide investors with further insight into Microsoft's cloud and Copilot developments as the company seeks to maintain its position in an increasingly competitive AI market.

data.title: Why SpaceX shares are sliding ahead of historic Starship Flight 15 launch?
data.description:
SpaceX SPCX shares fell on Friday ahead of a high-stakes Starship test flight, with investors also weighing growing scrutiny of Elon Musk's potential merger plans involving Tesla.

The stock traded 1% lower on Friday at around 11:45 AM EDT.

Major US indexes also moved lower, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq shedding over 1.6% as investors continued to digest headlines around outgoing Nvidia chief Jensen Huang

Tesla merger faces growing political scrutiny

One factor weighing on SpaceX was increased scrutiny of its potential merger with Tesla.

Bloomberg reported on Thursday that the companies could announce a deal as soon as December.

However, the changing political environment could bring greater scrutiny to merger discussions involving two of the state's most valuable companies.

At the federal level, Democrats who took control of Congress have signaled plans to investigate Musk's business and political activities.

Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has vowed to take a close look at the potential merger.

"Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny," Johnson told Bloomberg.

He also raised concerns about the concentration of private and public-sector influence around Musk.

"I don't want anybody to have such control of the public sector that they can bend public power to their private gain. I think his Empire is at great risk of crossing that line," Johnson said of Musk.

However, Johnson also indicated a willingness to have discussions with the world's richest man, who donated heavily, but in vain, to Republican causes during the midterm elections.

Analysts have also highlighted structural obstacles to combining the two companies, particularly the challenge of separating Tesla's substantial Chinese manufacturing operations from SpaceX's sensitive US defense contracts.

SpaceX restructures Grok Imagine team

Separately, SpaceX's AI division laid off roughly 60 employees from the Grok Imagine video-generation team, The Information reported on Friday.

The cuts leave only a small number of employees to maintain the image and video features of the Grok chatbot.

They form part of a restructuring following the earlier integration of xAI into SpaceX.

The move reflects a shift in resources toward coding tools and other priorities, while adding to questions about the future development of Grok's image and video-generation capabilities.

Starship Flight 15 becomes another major catalyst

Investors are also focused on Starship Flight 15, which is set to take place later on Friday.

The mission aims to achieve a historic recovery of both the Super Heavy booster and the upper-stage Starship using the launch tower's mechanical arms.

A successful recovery would mark an important advance in SpaceX's efforts to develop a rapidly reusable launch system.

It could also support denser Starlink deployments and the company's longer-term ambitions involving orbital computing infrastructure.

KeyBanc on Friday reiterated its Sector Weight rating on SpaceX, while expressing optimism about the upcoming Starship launch.

"The launch is a key milestone for the program, as SPCX seeks to demonstrate fixes and enhancements implemented following some anomalies encountered during Flight 14 in September 2026," the brokerage said.

Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas also reiterated an Overweight rating on SpaceX, maintaining his $300 price target.

Jonas described a successful catch of the Starship and Super Heavy booster as "one of the most significant potential catalysts in SpaceX's nearly 25-year history."

The upcoming flight therefore represents an important milestone for the company as it works to demonstrate the improvements made following Flight 14 and advance its reusable rocket program.

data.title: Analyst who warned about Nvidia and Jensen Huang flagged Ethereum price
data.description:
Ethereum price has intensified its sell-off today, reaching its lowest level since August 19 this year. It has now slumped by over 31.5% from its highest point in August this year, and technicals suggest that it has more downside to go. For one, Culper Research, the research shop that warned about Jensen Huang affair also warned about Ethereum. 

Culper Research warned about Ethereum

Jensen Huang made headlines this week after confirming that he had an affair with a Chinese national whom US intelligence officials believe to be a spy. The report led to his resignation on Thursday.

While the report has shocked Wall Street, it was nothing new to Culper Research, a New York firm that warned about the affair with Alice Huang in May.

Investors have now turned their attention to Culper’s other warnings, including one it issued against Ethereum in March. At the time, the firm said it was short Ethereum, the second-biggest cryptocurrency in the world. It also disclosed a short position on BitMine, the biggest Ethereum holder in the world.

In its report on Ethereum, Culper Research said that Ethereum was in a “death spiral” after last year’s Fusaka upgrade. One of the aspects is that base fees collected on Ethereum will continue falling, meaning that less ETH is burned under EIP-1559. As a result, that means that Ethereum’s deflationary story will keep weakening.

This view has been confirmed by the recent data by DeFi Llama. The numbers show that Ethereum has generated just $27.3 million in fees this quarter, down from $34 million in the previous quarter. In total, the chain has made $153 million this year, down from $523 million last year.

Further, while Ethereum wallet growth has intensified, Culper Research found that most of this was because of spam. Indeed, the analyst found that 22% of all Ethereum transactions were tied to address poisoning. 

The analyst also warned that Vitalik Buterin had continuing selling his ETH coins, a sign that he expects the coin to remain under pressure. 

Ethereum ETF outflows have soared

Fundamentals also explain why ETH price has continued falling. Data shows that spot Ethereum ETF outflows have surged in the past few weeks. They have lost over $766 million this month after losing $1.6 billion last month. In total, they have lost over $2.6 billion in this period, a sign that demand has continued to wane.

More data shows that Ethereum’s futures open interest has continued to fall. The daily figure dropped by 6.5% in the last 24 hours to $23.5 billion. At its peak this year, Ethereum had an open interest of over $60 billion. A falling open interest is a sign that investors expect the coin to continue dropping. 

Ethereum liquidations have jumped in the past few months as exchanges closed leveraged positions, leading to more pressure.

ETH price technical analysis

Ethereum price chart | Source: TradingView

Technicals suggest that ETH price has more downside to go. It is about to form a death cross pattern as the spread between the 50-day and 200-day moving averages narrowed. This death cross pattern normally points to more downside.

The coin has dropped below the 61.8% Fibonacci Retracement level, confirming more downside. Therefore, the path of the least resistance for the token is bearish, with the next target to watch being at $1,500. On the flip side, a move above the 50% retracement level of $2,157 will invalidate the bearish outlook.

The post Analyst who warned about Nvidia and Jensen Huang flagged Ethereum price appeared first on Invezz
